Travel nursing. I left Mission Trail in June 2020 and signed with Lonestar Traveler Staffing, which is a travel agency out of Houston, small, but my recruiter there was honestly great. I did travel ICU from July 2020 to August 2021. I've worked in like ten different hospitals because of it, it feels like, you lose track.

Okay actually let me count. It was four contracts. First one was Laredo, Texas, July to October 2020, a community hospital, their ICU was maybe 16 beds and they had turned a med-surg floor into overflow ICU too. Then El Paso, October 2020 into January 2021, I extended that one. El Paso was the worst thing I've ever seen as a nurse. That was the fall surge, they had the refrigerated trucks outside. Ratios were one to three, some nights one to four with vented patients, which is not safe, everybody knew it was not safe, and we did it anyway. The pay was the most I'll ever make as a nurse, I think it peaked around $4,800 a week, and I'd give it back. Well. Maybe not all of it.

Then Bakersfield, California, February to May 2021. California has the mandated ratios so it was one to two, it felt like a vacation compared to El Paso, which is a messed up thing to say about an ICU during COVID. And the last one was Tulsa, Oklahoma, May to August 2021. In Tulsa they actually had me in charge some shifts, which travelers usually don't get, because they were so short on core staff with experience. So four hospitals, four cities.

What travel teaches you is how to walk into a new unit and be useful in like a day. Every place had a different Epic build, or Cerner in Bakersfield, different policies, different everything. You get a four-hour orientation if you're lucky, and then you have patients. I got really fast at figuring out how a place actually works, like who really decides things, where the supplies are hidden, which doctor you call versus which one you page. I used to make myself a one-page cheat sheet for each hospital the first night. I still have them somewhere.

I also noticed every place was having the same problems. Staffing, obviously. But also the documentation, the handoffs, the same alerts everyone clicks through. Every hospital thought its mess was special, and it really wasn't.

By August 2021 I was done. Like, done done. I was having trouble sleeping, I'd hear the vent alarms when I was in the grocery store. I didn't renew in Tulsa and I went home to San Antonio. And then my mom had her hip replacement that October, she lives alone, so I moved back in with her for a few months and took care of her through the recovery and the PT. So I just didn't work. I took a real break, the first time since nursing school. Daniel was still in San Antonio then, this is before he got the Denver job. Then he got the offer in early 2022 and we moved to Denver in March 2022, and I didn't go back to work until July 2022 when I started at Foothill Peaks. So it was about ten or eleven months off, start to finish, September 2021 to July 2022.

People ask if I regret the travel part and no, I don't. I paid off my student loans and the rest of my car. I learned a lot. But it's also part of why I'm not going back to full-time bedside. I gave a lot already.

One more thing about the travel. In El Paso I ended up sort of informally running orientation for the newer travelers who came in after me, because I was there the longest and I knew the place. Nobody asked me to, it just happened. I made them the same cheat sheet I made for myself. I think I did that for maybe eight or ten nurses over those three months. It wasn't official at all, but they had me do it again in Tulsa.
